import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 886

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/886](https://www.erdosproblems.com/886)
- [ErRo97] Erdős, Paul and Rosenfeld, Moshe, The factor-difference set of integers. Acta Arith.
  (1997), 353--359.
-/

open Nat Filter

namespace Erdos886

/--
The set of divisors of $n$ in the interval $(n^{1/2}, n^{1/2} + n^{1/2-\epsilon})$.
-/
noncomputable def Erdos886Divisors (n : ℕ) (ε : ℝ) (C : ℝ) : Finset ℕ :=
  (divisors n).filter (fun d =>
    (n : ℝ) ^ (1/2 : ℝ) < d ∧ (d : ℝ) < (n : ℝ) ^ (1/2 : ℝ) + C * (n : ℝ) ^ (1/2 - ε))

/--
Let $\epsilon>0$. Is it true that, for all large $n$, the number of divisors of $n$ in
$(n^{1/2},n^{1/2}+n^{1/2-\epsilon})$ is $O_\epsilon(1)$?

Erdős attributes this conjecture to Ruzsa.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_886 :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ ε > 0, ∃ K : ℕ, ∀ᶠ n in atTop, (Erdos886Divisors n ε 1).card ≤ K := by
  sorry

/--
Erdős and Rosenfeld [ErRo97] proved that there are infinitely many $n$ such that there are
four divisors of $n$ in $(n^{1/2},n^{1/2}+16n^{1/4})$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_886.variants.rosenfeld_infinite :
    Set.Infinite {n | 4 ≤ (Erdos886Divisors n (1/4) 16).card} := by
  sorry

/--
Erdős and Rosenfeld [ErRo97] proved that, for any constant $C>0$, all large $n$ have at most
$1+C^2$ many divisors in $[n^{1/2}, n^{1/2}+Cn^{1/4}]$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_886.variants.rosenfeld_bound :
    ∀ C > 0, ∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in atTop,
    ((divisors n).filter (fun (d : ℕ) =>
      (n : ℝ) ^ (1 / 2 : ℝ) ≤ (d : ℝ) ∧ (d : ℝ) ≤ (n : ℝ) ^ (1 / 2 : ℝ) + C * (n : ℝ) ^ (1 / 4 : ℝ))).card
      ≤ 1 + C ^ 2 := by
  sorry

end Erdos886

findings.description: The docstring describes the interval (n^(1/2), n^(1/2) + n^(1/2−ε)), omitting the parameter C. The definition actually uses upper endpoint n^(1/2) + C·n^(1/2−ε). This matters when the helper is used with C = 16 in rosenfeld_infinite. For example, Lean verifies that Erdos886Divisors 16 (1/4) 16 = {8, 16}, whereas the unscaled interval described by the docstring contains no divisors of 16. The definition and theorem statements themselves are correct.
findings.source_evidence: https://www.erdosproblems.com/latex/886 distinguishes the main interval (n^(1/2), n^(1/2)+n^(1/2−ε)) from the infinitude variant's interval (n^(1/2), n^(1/2)+16n^(1/4)). The helper correctly accommodates both, but its docstring at line 33 describes only C = 1.
findings.suggested_fix: Change the definition's docstring to describe the interval $(n^{1/2}, n^{1/2} + C n^{1/2-\epsilon})$. Leave the Lean definition and theorem statements unchanged.

reformulations.difference: The source asks for an O_ε(1) bound; Lean instead existentially quantifies a natural-number bound K for the divisor count, holding eventually atTop.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For a natural-valued counting function f, its real norm equals its value. Thus f = O(1) is equivalent to an eventual real upper bound. Any such bound can be rounded upward to a natural K, and a natural bound is also a real bound. On ℕ, eventually atTop means that there exists N such that the bound holds for every n ≥ N. Placing ∀ ε > 0 before these witnesses permits precisely the ε-dependence required by O_ε(1). The full quantified equivalence was proved in the scratch file.

sources_consulted: https://www.erdosproblems.com/886 — read through https://r.jina.ai/https://www.erdosproblems.com/886 after direct requests were blocked.

Erdős, Paul and Rosenfeld, Moshe, The factor-difference set of integers, Acta Arithmetica 79(4) (1997), 353–359, especially Propositions 4.1–4.2 and the Ruzsa discussion on p. 358. Full paper read at https://matwbn.icm.edu.pl/ksiazki/aa/aa79/aa7944.pdf.
review.notes: All three theorem statements faithfully match the cited problem page, and their open/solved categories agree with it. Scratch checks in /workspace/review/scratch.lean compile without errors or warnings and verify the big-O equivalence, infinitude interpretation, n = 0 and n = 1 cases, scaling behavior, and open versus closed endpoints.
